title: Latency spike fingerprinting and quick isolation checklist
content:
Summary:

A concise working checklist and fingerprinting playbook for fast triage of evening/low-frequency latency spikes observed in Dedicated GPU pools. Target audience: oncall SRE and serving-runtime engineers doing first-response isolation and hypothesis capture. This is intentionally lightweight — the goal is to identify "fingerprints" (signal combinations) that map to likely root causes and to provide quick isolation actions that are reversible and low-risk.

Scope and motivation:
- Applies to Dedicated GPU pools serving multi-tenant inference (ephemeral slots + KV cache).
- Covers symptoms that look like sudden p95/p99 generator latency jumps (20–300% increase) with capacity still reporting nominal GPU utilization.
- Motivated by repeated evening regressions where noisy tenants or autoscaler hysteresis produced transient tail latency increases that cascaded to fallbacks.

Observed signals to collect immediately (first 10 minutes):
- p95/p99 request latency by pool and by tenant_id (if available). Metric names we use: "request_latency_ms.p95", "request_latency_ms.p99".
- Per-GPU metrics: gpu_util_pct, mem_used_gb, power_watts, temperature_c.
- PCIe/driver errors: pci_ecc_count, cuda_error_rate.
- Allocator/backpressure: allocator_queue_len, allocation_retries, pool_alloc_failures.
- KV cache signals: kv_cache_hit_rate, kv_cache_evictions_per_min, kv_cache_lookup_latency.
- Scheduling/placement: slot_placement_retries, affinity_rebalance_events.
- Autoscaler: desired_replicas, current_replicas, scale_events (timestamps).
- Host-level: CPU steal, oom_kills, host_load1.
- Logs: recent gcore/dmesg entries, docker/k8s container restarts for runner daemons.

Quick isolation checklist (fast, reversible actions — aim for <15 minutes):
1) Confirm scope: are all tenants affected or one/ few? Query request_latency by tenant_id and sample logs for impacted tenant(s).
   - If single tenant: likely noisy neighbor; proceed to step 2.
   - If broad: likely infra issue, autoscale, kernel/driver; jump to step 4.

2) Throttle suspected tenant(s) via soft policy (rate-limit keys):
   - Apply temporary rate limit to tenant API key (10–30% of normal) or pause their ingress to the pool.
   - Observe latency after 60–120s. If p95 drops, mark as "noisy-tenant confirmed" and continue isolation.

3) Evict tenant from pool (if rate-limit not possible):
   - Move the tenant to a maintenance pool or cordon nodes they run on for placement.
   - Monitor for p95 recovery. Record exact command and timestamp.

4) Check autoscaler signals and recent scale events:
   - Look for scaledown followed by up within short window (hysteresis bounce). If found, temporarily pin desired_replicas to current_replicas to prevent immediate oscillation while investigating.
   - If scale events coincide with latency spike, snapshot the node assignment and schedule for replay.

5) Rapid driver/host health check:
   - Run quick grep on dmesg for GPU/PCIe messages since spike start. Check nvidia-smi for ECC errors.
   - If host-level errors present on >1 host in the pool, open infra incident and escalate.

6) KV cache sanity check:
   - If kv_cache_evictions_per_min spikes and kv_cache_hit_rate drops, consider disabling prefetch for offending tenant or temporarily increase cache capacity for pool.

7) Minimal fallback/redeploy:
   - If no clear tenant and host health is clean, try rolling restart of the serving binary on 1-2 nodes (canary) to see if latency follows node.

Fingerprint patterns and likely mappings (empirical):
- Fingerprint A (Noisy-tenant with synchronous large batches): p99 up, gpu_util_pct high for single GPU, allocator_queue_len spike, pool_alloc_failures low, kv_cache_hit_rate unchanged. Likely cause: tenant issuing large sync jobs that block GPU and cause queueing. Mitigation: rate-limit, batch-size caps, tenant isolation.

- Fingerprint B (KV cache amplification / cache thrash): p95 up, kv_cache_evictions_per_min large, kv_cache_lookup_latency up, gpu_util_pct moderate. Likely cause: pathological prompt patterns causing many unique keys; mitigation: increase cache size temporarily, restrict tenant cache insert rate.

- Fingerprint C (Autoscaler oscillation): p95/p99 up across tenants, desired_replicas fluctuating in recent minutes, scale events aligned with latency spikes. Likely cause: hysteresis config too tight; mitigation: pin replicas and adjust cooldown/thresholds.

- Fingerprint D (Driver/host degradation): p50/p95 shift with GPU ECC or PCIe errors, host-level dmesg entries, multiple GPUs with thermal anomalies. Likely cause: driver regression or hardware fault. Mitigation: cordon hosts, escalate to infra/hardware, skip autoscale changes until resolved.

Deep triage checklist (post-isolation if not resolved):
- Collect flamegraphs/tracing for the affected timeframe (alloc-tracer traces).
- If noisy tenant suspected: fetch last N requests from tenant (sample size 50–200) and re-run through local cluster replay harness for performance profiling.
- Correlate scheduler logs with spike time to identify placement churn or affinity flaps.
- If autoscale: replay metric series into autoscaler simulator (link in linked_artifacts) to reproduce oscillation and test tuned hysteresis values.

Commands and short snippets to run (examples):
- Query p99 by tenant (datadog/prom query): "avg:last_5m:request_latency_ms.p99{pool:dedicated-east,tenant_id:*} by {tenant_id}"
- Check allocator queue: "sum:allocator_queue_len{pool:dedicated-east} by {host}"
- Quick host dmesg: "ssh host && sudo dmesg | tail -n 200 | egrep 'NVRM|GPU|PCI'"
- Temporarily pin autoscaler: POST /internal/autoscaler/override {"pool": "dedicated-east", "replicas": 12, "ttl": 1800} (internal admin API)

Oncall notes / example timeline (real incident skeleton):
- 20:03 UTC — p99 on pool "dedicated-east" rose from 280ms -> 1.1s. Alerts triggered.
- 20:05 UTC — Confirmed impact primarily for tenant T-834 and T-921.
- 20:06 UTC — Soft throttle applied to T-834 (30% of normal throughput). p99 dropped to 420ms in 90s.
- 20:12 UTC — KV cache eviction rate for pool spiked 8x; suspected cache thrash for T-921.
- 20:20 UTC — Evict T-921 to maintenance pool; overall p99 recovered to baseline by 20:26.
- Post-incident: follow-up revealed a customer traffic pattern with many short-lived variable-length prompts caused cache blowout.

Post-incident action items (examples to assign):
- Investigate adaptive cache admission to prevent thrash (owner: Miguel S.).
- Add per-tenant cache-insert rate control (owner: Priya N.).
- Autoscaler tuning: increase scale cooldown to 3m and test in simulator (owner: Jon R.).
- Improve alerting: add cross-metric rule to only alert when p99 and pool_alloc_failures co-occur to reduce noise (owner: Claire Z.).

Open questions / things to validate:
- Are tenant throttles visible in user-facing billing telemetry? (need to ensure customer impact tracked)
- Should we implement a protection that auto-applies a mild global per-tenant rate limit when evictions > X within Y minutes?
- What is acceptable MTTI for dedicated pool driver-level failures? SLA implication check needed.

Notes to self (fragile ideas / hypotheses):
- Consider a lightweight "fingerprint id" label emitted when we detect pattern matches A-D above; include fingerprint id in incident notes for faster future triage.
- Explore instrumenting allocator to expose per-tenant allocation latency percentiles; would help separate tenant-induced queueing from host problems.

References and quick links:
- Autoscaler simulator notebook: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SRE/Autoscaler+Simulator
- Alloc tracer PR used in replay: https://github.com/redwood-inference/alloc-tracer/pull/142
- Related Jira: SRE-2124 (evening latency spikes), INFRA-789 (PCIe error investigation)

If you run this doc during an oncall, please append a short incident timeline and the predicates you used to choose each isolation action (helps build the fingerprint bank).

-- Claire Z.

(End of draft checklist — feedback welcome; next: convert into a small runbook page and wire up quick admin buttons for throttle/override.)
